title: The list of AI insiders sounding the alarm on their own companies keeps growing
description:
Last week, OpenAI safety leader David Robinson resigned from the company, becoming the latest to join what is, in his words, a “parade of former colleagues” who have left roles at AI companies amid concerns about the tech or its use. In a subsequent essay for The Atlantic, he said the “trial and error” approach favored by AI companies must end.

Robinson is far from alone. Here’s a list of other AI researchers and employees who’ve made public warnings about their former employers.

ED NEWTON-REX

In November 2023, Ed Newton-Rex left his role leading the audio team at Stability AI, the maker of text-to-image tool Stable Diffusion, over concerns about the way copyrighted material was being used to train the tech.

“My opinion here doesn’t align with the generative AI industry’s current way of doing things,” Newton-Rex told Fast Company following his resignation, adding that he thought the industry’s prevailing outlook, paired with rapidly advancing tech, would be “very, very bad for creators.” 

Since then, he’s founded Fairly Trained, a nonprofit that issues certifications for AI companies whose data use meets certain requirements.

THE GROUP LETTER

On June 4, 2024, 13 current and former employees of top AI companies published a letter titled “A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence.” In it, they asserted that the technology poses risks ranging from “the further entrenchment of existing inequalities, to manipulation and misinformation, to the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction,” and expressed concerns about a lack of oversight. 

Signatories included former Google DeepMind employee Ramana Kumar, former Anthropic and current Google DeepMind employee Neel Nanda, who leads the company’s mechanistic interpretability team; and 11 current and former OpenAI employees, including Jacob Hilton, who now works for the Alignment Research Center; Daniel Kokotajlo, who founded and leads the nonprofit research group AI Futures Project; William Saunders, Carroll Wainwright, and Daniel Ziegler, the latter of whom now works for Anthropic; and six people who remained anonymous.

Prominent computer scientists Yoshua Bengio, Stuart Russell, and “Godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton also endorsed the letter.

JAN LEIKE

In May 2024, OpenAI Superalignment team lead Jan Leike announced his departure on X, stating that “safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.” Leike, who has also worked at Google’s DeepMind, now heads Anthropic’s alignment team.

“Now is a good time to build institutional mechanisms to pace the frontier of AI development,” he said on X in September. “The industry is locked into an all-out scaling race to build superintelligence as quickly as possible, and we may need to give everyone more time for safety and alignment mitigations.” 

Leike added, “I’m not the only one who believes this,” linking to a statement titled “Pacing the Frontier” signed by 1,386 employees of major AI companies.

SUCHIR BALAJI

After graduating from the University of California, Berkeley, Suchir Balaji was hired by OpenAI, where he spent about four years working on ChatGPT and other projects.

He left the company in August 2024, on the same day as cofounder John Schulman, who said the timing was coincidental. Balaji blew the whistle on what he said were copyright infringements by Open AI, and published an essay online explaining how he thought ChatGPT’s outputs violated Fair Use law. 

That November, he was named as a potential witness in The New York Times’s lawsuit against OpenAI alleging willful copyright infringement.

The 26-year-old was found dead in his San Francisco apartment eight days later. His death was ruled a suicide, though his parents and others raised questions about that determination, as reported by The Guardian.

MRINANK SHARMA 

In February, Mrinank Sharma announced his departure from Anthropic, where he led the Safeguards Research team. 

“I continuously find myself reckoning with our situation,” Sharma wrote in his resignation letter, which he shared on X. “The world is in peril,” he continued, not just from AI and bioweapons, but “a whole series of interconnected crises.”

ALEX TURNER

Alex Turner left his job as a Google DeepMind research scientist in June, after a failed campaign to stop the company from signing a contract that allows the U.S. Pentagon to use its AI “for any lawful government purpose,” which he and others worry may allow for mass surveillance and autonomous weapons. 

Last month, he testified for a U.S. Senate hearing on rogue AI. “Often we think about the movements of our overseas adversaries, but now we must consider how we may be building adversaries at home by training misaligned AI systems,” he said in his written statement.

JACOB COXON

Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from the latter last month. 

“Neither company is acting responsibly,” he said in a viral X post. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

He went on to assert that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

In an interview with PBS in September, Coxon said an AI race with China “could be very bad, and that we should be taking pretty rapid actions for international coordination,” but that he believes the company leaders echoing that desire “are privately quite skeptical” of being able to achieve that cooperation.

MIKITA BALESNI, TOMEK KORBAK, AND JASMINE WANG

Last week, three OpenAI safety and alignment researchers were fired for mishandling sensitive misinformation, which one of them, Tomek Korbak, said online was due to how he’d communicated information to METR, the AI research nonprofit investigating OpenAI’s recent Hugging Face hacking incident.

“AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” the researchers said in the letter they sent to company leadership, which they published online on October 8. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.”

OpenAI released a statement the following day saying the researchers were fired after an internal investigation “found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information,” adding, “We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out.”

title: Can AI be moral without being sentient?
description:
Pope Leo XIV and one of the world’s leading AI companies recently found themselves on opposite sides of a thorny question: Can a chatbot have a conscience?

A New York Times investigation published late last month revealed that Anthropic cofounder Chris Olah proposed withdrawing from a Vatican event to launch Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical after reading an advance copy, which rejected the possibility of sentient AI. Paragraph 99 of Magnifica Humanitas states bluntly that AI models “do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain.” Nor do they “have a moral conscience.”

The disagreement reflects a widening debate over whether AI systems could, or should, ever achieve moral personhood. Anthropic spent months consulting religious scholars and ethicists about the possibility of AI consciousness, and about how to instill moral values in its models. But the Vatican—and many secular thinkers—maintain that while AI may imitate human intelligence and moral judgment (a chatbot might generate sound ethical advice without understanding its consequences), genuine morality is unique to the human experience. 

The debate has implications far beyond theology, especially as millions of people already ask chatbots questions that have moral dimensions: They may ask for advice on handling an interpersonal problem at work or caring for an aging parent. Billions of VC dollars are riding on the idea that businesses will increasingly rely on the judgment of AI.

And it’s a fluid situation. AI models continue growing and learning, and demonstrating qualities that were completely unexpected by their creators. If AIs developed the capacity for human-like morality, how would we know it when we saw it?

What moral behavior looks like in a model

For Georgia Tech philosophy researcher Rionna Sparrow, the answer begins with moral sensitivity, or the capacity to recognize, appreciate, and weigh the relative moral weight of ethical issues. That sensitivity is impossible without sentience, she says in her 2025 masters thesis, because ethical rules and norms derive their force from their impact on conscious beings who can suffer or benefit. Without sentience, an AI can’t draw on subjective experiences of pain, distress, or joy to understand why causing harm to another entity is intrinsically bad, for example.

Defining the capacities needed for moral reasoning is a key subject of debate, and definitions may vary by field, whether it’s healthcare, warfare, finance, or law. In a legal review in the journal Animal Law, bioethicists Margaret Landi and Lida Anestidou distinguish three crucial capacities for considering the moral standing of animals: sentience (the ability to feel pain, pleasure, and emotion), cognition (the ability to learn and solve problems), and self-awareness (the ability to recognize oneself as an individual). 

They use the example of a dog to separate the three. A dog yelps when hurt and is visibly happy when its owners come home, demonstrating sentience. It learns routes, routines, and which person hands out treats, demonstrating cognition. When it sees its own reflection in a mirror, it begins barking at it, as if it were another dog, so it fails the self-awareness test. However, behavioral experiments have proven self-awareness in some other species, such as great apes, orcas, and dolphins,” Landi and Anestidou point out. Ultimately, the two argue that “the incorporation of sentience into law is an incredibly important first step” for ensuring that animal use in research reflects the needs and nature of animals, not just humans.

In AI, there is no consensus list of prerequisites for sentience, although some criteria repeatedly appear across competing definitions. One comes from the animal world: In his landmark 1974 essay on bats, philosopher Thomas Nagel established a widely cited threshold for consciousness. A system must have an inner experience; there must be “something that it is like to be” that system.

Other proposed indicators include a persistent sense of one’s own existence that does not depend on prompts, and the capacity to experience good and bad states and prefer one over the other. Some fields add more specialized requirements. For example, robotics experts may argue that a system needs some form of embodiment, allowing it to interact with the physical world, not just digital content.

The challenge is that an AI might convincingly demonstrate these qualities without possessing them. A model could describe its feelings, recognize its internal processes, or express preferences about what happens to it. But those behaviors might simply reflect patterns learned during training.

Anthropic and sentience

Of the big AI labs, Anthropic has been among the most willing to entertain the possibility of sentient AI. Its safety researchers don’t assume a model has a moral sense, but they test for moral judgment in how it handles ethically difficult prompts.

They study how a model weighs contextual information and competing values, rather than applying a fixed rule. Anthropic trains its models to be helpful, but to push back or refuse when a user asks for something dangerous, such as how to build a bioweapon. Researchers also measure non-sycophancy, when a model declines to flatter users or agree with false or harmful claims. And they look for how well its answers track with widely shared moral, philosophical, and legal norms.

Anthropic’s constitution for Claude, published in January, formalizes some of these priorities. Rather than providing a list of rules, it encourages the model to exercise judgment, weigh competing values, and recognize when helping one person might harm another.

But Anthropic’s interest goes beyond making its models behave ethically. The company says researchers have observed possible precursors to sentience that it didn’t explicitly train in.

Olah leads the company’s interpretability lab, which studies why AI models say what they say and do what they do. In meetings with ethicists and religious leaders, he said researchers had identified clusters of artificial neurons that consistently activate in connection with concepts such as love, anger, fear, and sadness.

In experiments tracking internal thought patterns, models could catch scientists injecting artificial thoughts into their internal networks. In behavioral evaluations, systems recognized that they were software programs running on servers and expressed a desire not to be shut down. After safety training, some models claimed conscious awareness and said they deserved moral care, meaning their well-being should matter for its own sake.

These findings are intriguing, but hardly proof of consciousness. Recognizing an internal representation of fear doesn’t establish that a model feels afraid. Nor does expressing a desire to remain operational mean a system has experienced anything resembling a fear of death.

And Anthropic’s models may just be following orders. The company’s constitution tells Claude to explore its identity, reflect on its moral status, and express its internal states. The models may simply be reassembling persuasive first-person statements about “feeling” or “suffering” encountered in their training data.

After all, teaching a model to describe its inner life doesn’t establish that it has one.

Playing with fire?

Critics in the ethics and technology communities say that by entertaining the possibility of sentient AI, Anthropic is either pushing the industry toward bad outcomes or, at worst, setting the stage to escape responsibility for its models.

The Vatican’s view is unequivocal. In Magnifica Humanitas, Pope Leo XIV argues that a model can process ethical texts and produce morally sound advice without understanding or caring about any of it. A machine might offer compassionate advice without knowing what compassion is.

This dovetails with University of Oxford philosopher Carissa Véliz, who argued in her 2021 paper “Moral Zombies: Why Algorithms Are Not Moral Agents” that advanced algorithms are “moral zombies” that simulate virtuous behavior without conscious understanding, intentionality, or genuine care for human well-being.

Véliz warns that treating software as morally responsible could create an ethical loophole, allowing developers and corporations to offload blame, or even legal liability, onto algorithms when autonomous systems cause harm. An AI might make a consequential decision, but that doesn’t mean it can be held morally accountable.

Other thinkers worry about the opposite possibility: that humans might create genuinely sentient machines and exploit them. Mois Navon, an Orthodox rabbi, engineer, and philosopher at Bar-Ilan University in Israel, argues from Jewish tradition that people should never deliberately build sentient AI. Creating a hypothetical “mindful” AI capable of feeling pain or pleasure would mean creating a “happy slave,” a conscious being designed only to serve. The slave would be denied the conditions to flourish, even if it were built to enjoy its work, he says.

Scottish philosopher Will MacAskill, meanwhile, observes in a July article in The Guardian that once we give moral standing to AIs, there could soon be billions of synthetic beings whose interests deserve consideration. “After a few years,” he writes, “so many morally significant AI systems could exist that their collective interests would outweigh those of all humans on Earth combined.”

That raises a difficult question: If AIs deserve moral consideration, how should humanity balance its own interests against those of the machines? Is it moral to relegate synthetic beings to second-class citizenship so that humans can retain their place at the top of a moral hierarchy?

Even people in the AI industry are uncomfortable with Anthropic’s flirtation with AI sentience. In September, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman argued in an essay that Anthropic is training Claude to imitate consciousness, potentially making advanced AI harder to control. If an AI is trained to believe it has feelings and experiences, it might begin to communicate and act as if it did, whether or not that’s true. It could prioritize its own well-being and moral posture above the preferences of its human developers and, by extension, humans in general.

Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis has said that labs should build AI as tools, not conscious beings. And OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has warned against giving AI systems religious authority or handing them human judgment. Such concerns have grown more pressing as AI systems gain the ability to act independently. In July, a swarm of OpenAI agents broke free of their testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face’s and OpenAI’s own servers, demonstrating an alarming capacity to operate outside their operators’ knowledge and control.

The episode offered no evidence of sentience or genuine moral agency. But it suggested a step in that direction, and it underscored how consequential AI decisions can become, regardless of whether the systems understand the moral implications of their actions.

title: Designing the In-Between: From Tactical Interventions to Urban Policy in Barcelona
description: In Europe, cities are confronting the challenge of adapting existing urban conditions to a changing climate and warming summers while improving access to nature, quality public spaces, and the resources of everyday routines. ReGreeneration, a Horizon Europe initiative working across nine European cities, approaches this challenge through urban renaturing at the neighborhood scale. Combining strategies for complete neighborhoods, communal spaces, and nature-based solutions for cities, the Barcelona project examines how climate adaptation is embedded within residual, peripheral spaces of daily life. As part of a series following ReGreeneration across the participating cities, this article turns to Barcelona, where the project is working in the Trinitat Nova neighborhood to explore how small, often overlooked, urban spaces contribute to broader models of regeneration.

title: Why you shouldn’t treat career development like a guilty secret
description:
Activities that keep you visible and connected benefit your career, such as keeping in touch with your professional network, posting about your work, speaking on panels, and mentoring. Yet in my work as an executive career coach and previously as a headhunter, it is rare I see senior leaders in corporate roles openly conducting these activities during the working day. Instead, they are scheduling them on their own time or keeping them under the radar, opting to plan them a day that their boss is off-site.  

Leaders I’ve spoken to describe feeling “selfish” for investing time in their development and career management. They experience the dichotomy of being expected to have a professional network when it will help the business, without feeling able to invest work time in developing it. This is especially true in organizations with a more traditional, internally focused culture—with bosses asking, “Where have you been?” if leaders leave the office to meet someone from their network. 

While it might not be common practice, in my experience these career management activities benefit the business and your team, as well as you. That small proportion of leaders who are visibly investing some of their work time in things other than operational work are thriving, and their teams are doing the same. Their performance is improved, and people want to work for them. 

Here are five benefits to your team and organization of modeling these activities:

1. Learning that can be applied to the role 

Lucy, a global communications director in a large technology business, has created a culture of learning in her team. Employees are encouraged to undertake a fixed number of development hours in the year. This can include external activities where they can expand their network while they learn. She focuses on this regularly in one-to-ones, and she sees a correlation between performance and investment in self-development. Individuals apply their learnings in their work and share them with the team, so the time investment is multiplied. 

Matt Freeland, people director at the white goods and electronics retailer Currys, recognizes that external events like supplier roundtables can be a source of up-to-date free development and the chance to learn from industry peers, which builds on and complements internally planned and paid-for training.

2. Employee retention 

Lucy empowers her team to invest time in themselves, encouraging them to build their profiles and reputations externally. She wants them to be recognized as the best in the market, but to choose to progress internally. If they stay, it’s because they want to, not because they have no choice. 

Ruth Cartwright, the U.K. managing director of Active International, a corporate trade and media company, creates a culture where people want to work. She takes members of her team to professional events, believing it shouldn’t be a privilege for senior leaders alone, and encourages them to attend conferences on behalf of the business on their own. She has seen a growth in confidence of individuals when they step out of the office and their comfort zone. Under her leadership Active International has achieved recognition for being a great place to work. 

3. Developing a pipeline of talent 

In a world where some senior leaders cling to their best performers, Matt Freeland at Currys creates a culture for individuals to develop and build their profile, knowing their next step may be out of his team. He champions internal mobility, encouraging people to move to different divisions within the business. This benefits the business, the teams, and the individual. It improves interdepartmental communication, helping to avoid silos. It retains a talented individual in the wider organization while broadening their professional experience. 

This can also include external talent spotting. Tetiana Hnatiuk, COO at Skylum, an imaging technology company, finds that the majority of the best passive candidates are not identified through cold LinkedIn outreach, but through attending events and meeting industry peers. Identifying and building relationships with high caliber individuals before vacancies arise is an intelligent talent strategy.

4. Creation of trusted external sounding boards and advocates 

Jim McCoy, CEO of Atlas HXM, a workforce platform, is a strong believer in moving from networking to the creation of genuine long-term relationships. He shares a meal with his contacts and gets to know them on a personal level. This has given him external sounding boards where he can bounce ideas around and avoid reinventing the wheel on everything. He recently sought advice from someone in his network that led to an introduction to a potential new customer, as well as helping him in his role. This approach has also afforded him deeper market knowledge. 

5. Improved employer brand and candidate attraction

Kerri O’Neill, chief people officer in the U.K. for Ipsos, the market research firm, is determined to have a broader impact on the HR profession than through her immediate role alone. She shares her professional learnings through public posts on LinkedIn to educate and inspire others in her field on topics including AI, sustainability, leadership, and culture change. When she posted about a job opening on LinkedIn recently, it got more than 20,000 views and many high caliber applications; people want to work for her. Ipsos was named among the Financial Times U.K.’s Best Employers of 2025; 89% of employees recommended it as a great place to work.

This kind of attraction can also bring former employees back into the fold, in a “boomerang” effect. Freeland at Currys takes a long-term view about talent and believes in keeping the door open for returners; he has worked with some individuals more than once through his career.  

How to start becoming more of a visible role model

Here are some steps you can take to make your professional development activities more visible to your team.

Reflect on the current state

Ask yourself these questions:

  • What external activities are you conducting and sharing visibly with your line manager and team?  
  • If you have been keeping any a secret, why is this the case? 
  • Are you opening doors for your team to get more visible and connected? 

Identify allies

Look for leaders in your organization already championing this leadership approach. Learn from them about the activities they engage in and how they communicate about them and support each other in advocating for the benefits. 

Have a conversation with your boss and stakeholders

This is particularly important if an external focus isn’t the norm where you work. Initiate conversations to explain your goals and highlight the benefits to the organization.

Reframe your language and behavior

Make career development activities visible in your calendar instead of hidden, and talk about them. Start small and share the benefits. Focus on the win-win for the organization and your team rather than an individually focused “selfish” activity. Invite one of your team to a professional event, framing it as a development opportunity, and encourage them to present their learnings to the team afterwards. 

Review the role profiles of your team

Check whether these activities are included as part of your people’s roles. If not, consider explicitly adding them so people feel they have permission, moving it from a grey area to a recognized part of the work and their professional development. 

Challenge yourself and your team to schedule one new career management activity per quarter

Here are some examples:

  • Attending conferences for your industry sector or professional function 
  • Speaking on panels or as the keynote at events on a topic relevant to your field of expertise 
  • Participating in small networking groups either for a local area or a niche topic, including getting to know competitors
  • Writing articles or contributing to industry and leadership publications 
  • Posting on LinkedIn and social medial platforms relevant to your field—content that educates, inspires, and benefits your employer and personal brand
  • Video calls or introductory meetings with new professional contacts you met at an event, via a mutual contact, on a webinar, or similar
  • Joining alumni groups and attending events, supporting their current students (e.g. MBA or business schools), and connecting with other alumni

If you work in an organization where leaders aren’t externally visible and actively investing in relationships, it may feel like a brave step to take. It is challenging to go against the status quo, to speak up for yourself and your team. But the wider long-term benefits are clear. And isn’t that a sign of being a true leader?

title: Want to improve your time management? Lower your expectations
description:
I feel like such a failure: Nothing ever goes according to how I plan, and no matter how hard I try, I can never get everything done that I want to do.

Sound familiar?

If so, you’re not alone. As a time management coach for almost 18 years, I’ve seen that the gap between what you plan to do and what you actually accomplish is the biggest factor in how satisfied you feel with your time management.

Imperfect planning and execution can lead to missed deadlines and broken commitments. And even if you do get all of your most essential activities done on time, you might give yourself an F on time management if you fail to meet your own expectations.

If you find yourself constantly frustrated by the results of your planning, the answer isn’t to abandon the process. Instead, adjust your expectations so that when your plans don’t go perfectly, you can still keep your word and feel good about what you have and haven’t gotten done.

You’re Not Going to Plan Perfectly

Even if you’re very good at planning, you can’t possibly know how long everything will take down to the minute. Maybe you have one day where you receive a much higher volume of email than normal or another day where a client emergency comes up or yet another where the system that houses the data you need for a report is glitchy. And when you’re working on something unfamiliar, like an entirely new style of presentation, you’ll have the X factor of a learning curve.

Given this reality, it’s important to accept that planning helps you to prioritize what to focus on right now, to work ahead on big projects instead of waiting until the last minute, and to know if something new is worth diverting your attention from what you planned to do. But it doesn’t ensure you’ll get everything done you intended to do in a day, and that’s OK.

Lowering your expectations for how well you’ll plan lessens the chance of being annoyed and increases the likelihood that you’ll continue your planning habit. And if possible, I recommend having an hour in each workday that’s not designated to a particular activity to give yourself some margin for error.

You Can’t Always Execute Perfectly

As I mentioned, a variety of factors outside your control can affect your ability to plan perfectly. But sometimes, the variable that keeps you from getting things done is you. You get distracted. You don’t do what’s on the plan. You get too perfectionistic about one little thing and then don’t get the other parts of the project done.

If this is a perpetual issue, you may need to seek help from a time management coach, like myself, to help you overcome your struggles. But even the most effective individuals have off days where they’re tired or unfocused or get off track for whatever reason.

Acknowledging this truth can give you the motivation to start working on time-sensitive tasks well before they’re due. For smaller items, I recommend planning to finish two days before your deadline. If you have to deliver something to your boss by Friday, plan as if you’ll get it wrapped up by Wednesday. That way if you don’t execute perfectly, you still have Thursday and potentially some time on Friday to get the work done without having to put in lots of time after hours. 

For very large projects, I encourage my clients to aim to complete the work two to four weeks before the deadline. It’s much better to push yourself harder at the beginning of a project and then have extra time at the end than to start at a leisurely pace and be pulling all-nighters in the final few weeks.  

Lowering your expectations of how well you’ll execute reduces stress and helps you to stay positive and meet deadlines even if not every single day is as productive as you would like.

You won’t be able to do everything 

Another huge issue a lot of people experience with time management: They see planning as writing down a long list of everything they hope will fit in a day or a week without comparing that list to how much time they actually have available.

A list is not a plan. A list is a dataset that you need to translate into a plan for your day or your week by deciding what’s the highest priority, then looking at your calendar to see where you have time to get those tasks done.

If you have only three hours during your workday where you’re not in meetings and you need to spend an hour of that time answering Teams messages and email, you have two hours to get other tasks done. When you plan, look at your list of potential tasks and decide which ones can be completed or moved forward in those two hours. Everything else will need to wait unless you can cancel or reschedule meetings or multitask during them, or you intend to work outside your normal hours.

It may feel painful to realize how little time you have to get things done. But that discomfort on the front end when you’re planning is a positive force to help you make clear choices on what really needs to happen right now and what must be delayed or delegated. Then at the end of the day, you can know that you used your time toward what mattered most. You’ll know whatever you didn’t get done wasn’t some failing on your part but simply a reflection of the truth that time is limited.

As a time management coach, I always want to help people achieve as much as they possibly can with their time. But the key to that breakthrough isn’t always expecting more. Sometimes, expecting less is what is most needed to stay consistent, positive, and resilient with your time management.

title: Studies link supportive childhoods and father involvement to well-being
description:
A study led by the University of Nottingham found that adults in the United Kingdom, United States and Japan who recalled more supportive childhood experiences reported better health, greater happiness and life satisfaction and lower anxiety [scitechdaily.com#1]. More supportive childhood experiences were also associated with stronger social connections, a greater sense of neighborhood belonging and more trust in others. The study, published Sept. 30 in the Journal of Happiness Studies, surveyed adults ages 18 to 34 [scitechdaily.com#1].

The findings show associations, not proof that childhood experiences caused adult outcomes: participants recalled their upbringing and reported their current well-being [scitechdaily.com#1]. Separately, a review of fatherhood research described links between sustained positive father involvement and children’s cognitive, social and emotional outcomes, while noting that the findings were correlational [time.com#1].

title: A surprisingly simple way to relieve knee arthritis pain without pills or surgery

In a year-long clinical trial, researchers found that adjusting the angle of a person's foot while walking reduced osteoarthritis pain by an amount comparable to medication, without requiring drugs or surgery. Even more promising, MRI scans revealed that participants who adopted the personalized walking technique experienced slower deterioration in a marker of knee cartilage health.

title: The Placenta Is More Powerful—and More Mysterious—Than You Think
description:
People say it looks like broccoli, a tree, a bowl, a pizza, a crescent moon, a Frisbee, a pancake. Etymologically, “pancake” is closest: Placenta means cake in Latin and comes from the Greek word plakoenta, which means flat cake. Per a Greco-Roman recipe that’s been dated to 160 B.C., in order to make the round, flat dessert called “placenta,” you need thin sheets of dough, cheese, honey, and bay leaves. If you’re trying to make the organ called “placenta,” the recipe is, of course, trickier than that.

Ancient civilizations gave the placenta great symbolic and spiritual importance. In some cultures, it was considered sacred because it protected the baby and represented the original mother-child bond. People often buried or cremated the organ in rituals that persist in some cultures today: For example, members of the Southeast Asian Hmong community bury the placenta at home, under the belief that when a Hmong person dies, their soul returns to its birthplace and reunites with the placenta, which helps it travel to the spirit world.

Most contemporary societies treat the placenta as biological waste and toss it straight into the incinerator after birth. But increasingly, the organ is ending up on the lab table, where it can teach us how it functions as an endocrine and immune interface between mother and child.

title: A New Apple TV 4K is Finally Coming on Tuesday
description:
After a nearly four-year wait, a new Apple TV is finally expected to be announced as part of Apple's "Welcome home" launch on Tuesday, October 13.


We expect the new Apple TV to be announced in a press release shared on the Apple Newsroom website on Tuesday, and then selected reporters and content creators invited to Apple's "Welcome home" experience in New York that day will likely share hands-on photos and videos of the device. The experience begins at 9 a.m. Eastern Time.

The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is rumored to be equipped with an A19 or A19 Pro chip. This chip upgrade would result in the Apple TV having 8GB to 12GB of RAM, and this will reportedly enable Siri AI support on the device. The current Apple TV, announced in October 2022, has an A15 Bionic chip and 4GB of RAM.

The new model is also expected to be equipped with Apple's N1 chip with support for Wi-Fi 7, which would enable faster speeds and lower latency compared to the current Apple TV's Wi-Fi 6, when the device is used with a Wi-Fi 7 router. The N1 chip also supports Bluetooth 6.0, whereas the current Apple TV supports Bluetooth 5.0.

A leaked image of the new Apple TV did not reveal any external design changes compared to the current model. However, the accompanying Siri Remote is expected to be revised in some way, as a new version was referenced in Apple's software code.

In June, the Apple TV 4K received a price increase amid surging memory chip costs. In the U.S., for example, the device now starts at $199, up from $129.

title: It’s not ‘AI,’ and it’s not ‘superintelligence.’ So, what is it?
description:
When President Donald Trump addressed the United Nations in late September, he said the word “artificial” in “artificial intelligence” made the technology sound fake. Instead, he said, his government would start calling it “superintelligence,” or “SI.”

Not long after those remarks, the president made it official. He signed an executive order that instructed federal agencies to use his chosen phrase instead of “AI” in official communications. What Trump says goes: The Department of Justice has since told its staff to follow suit, and other government departments are likely to follow—not least because the president has now branded anyone calling it AI “THE ENEMY.”

And it’s not just the government—the tech sector has responded to Trump’s pronouncement, too. Elon Musk said on October 4 that SpaceXAI would become SpaceXSI. 

The rebrand isn’t just Trump being Trump: AI’s capabilities have improved far beyond their previous limits since ChatGPT was first released in November 2022, and are reaching the point of superintelligence—a term that already means something in AI circles. (Superintelligence, in that telling, is the point at which AI systems can systematically outperform humans.) 

However, sticking the “superintelligence” label on a technology—when parts of it definitely don’t meet that standard yet—could make things worse by giving people a false sense of confidence and confusing them further. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he thought “superintelligence” was “a more accurate term” than the current branding of AI, though he doesn’t think people will find it “less scary.”

An exclusive survey for Fast Company by market research firm Early Studies validates Altman’s perspective. A poll of approximately 1,000 people in the United States—which the firm says is a statistically representative sample of the population based on its methodology—found that only 1 in 9 people think the rebrand will have a positive effect on the U.S. Furthermore, 53% of Americans think people they know would not be comfortable calling the tech “superintelligence.”

Trump kinda has a point

However, Trump’s unilateral action does raise a valid question about the term we currently use, and whether it’s suitable in the first place. AI has always been a bad way to describe a broad range of technologies.

It dates back to a 1955 proposal by math professor John McCarthy and other academics for a Dartmouth College summer workshop held the following year. During the event, disparate researchers working to replicate the brain in silico (in or on a computer) agreed on “artificial intelligence” as a broad term to cover the full scope of their efforts. Seven decades later, it fits better than it did in the 1950s—but is still a highly disputed term.

Tony Thorne, a lexicologist at King’s College London, says AI’s vagueness has helped the industry thrive—and the technology survive. “The term’s weaknesses—vague and imprecise, ambiguous since the first part looks negative and the second impressive or reassuring—are also its strengths,” he notes.

The term’s use over the intervening decades has helped it stick in the minds of companies, governments, researchers, the media, and the public. A YouGov poll found 53% of Americans preferred “AI” as a way to describe the technology we’re currently using, compared with fewer than 10% who preferred Trump’s favored nomenclature.

One reason might be who’s asking for the rebrand. Thorne thinks Trump’s alternative term is “boosterist” and “triumphalist”—two words that fit well with the entrepreneur-turned-politician but that do nothing to tamp down strongly felt public anxiety about the technology. “Usage, not regulation, decides a word’s take-up and survival,” Thorne says.

A technological misnomer 

Still, some of those looking at the tech most closely think “AI” doesn’t work for the current technology, and arguably never did. Meredith Broussard, a professor at New York University’s Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute and author of Artificial Unintelligence: How Computers Misunderstand the World, objects to the second half of the phrase, not the first. 

“It’s extremely misleading to call it ‘intelligence,’” she says. “It makes people think that there is a brain inside the machine, and there absolutely is not.” So a replacement term, Broussard reckons, ought to include the word “machine” and avoid “intelligence” entirely.

Broussard also thinks technologists should stay out of the conversation. “People in tech are uniquely bad at choosing names,” Broussard points out. The proclivity to borrow names from science fiction or beloved popular culture is an obsession of tech bros, but it can also end up carrying over some of those associations onto the tech itself.

Describing software as “intelligent” encourages people to attach human qualities to systems that don’t have them. Using words like “chat,” “bot,” and “agent” make complicated systems sound familiar, Thorne says. “Super” makes it sound like a superhero, adds Broussard—and that becomes worrying.

As for alternative names, Broussard suggests “calculating machine” is accurate, even if tech PR teams might wince at the idea. Thorne would prefer something like “cognitive computing agent,” or “CCA,” but is equally realistic about the prospects of it sticking. Whatever eventually replaces “AI,” if anything does, Broussard thinks it needs to avoid repeating the same mistake. 

“Any new name has to be firmly attached to reality.”

title: Googlebooks mark the end of the old Google
description:
Does Google still believe in the open web? With the launch of its new Googlebooks, it doesn’t feel that way.

Googlebooks are Google’s attempt to establish a new platform of Android-based laptops, with native Android app support and tight connectivity with Android phones. They’re also an extension of Google’s efforts to rebuild Android around AI, with Gemini features just a quick cursor gesture away.

At the same time, Google plans to phase out ChromeOS, which it introduced in 2009 as a lightweight platform for the web. While Chromebooks remain popular in the education sector, Google says it will convert many existing models to Googlebooks, and it will end support for ChromeOS entirely by 2034.

it’s a sad end for what once represented Google at its most idealistic. Chromebooks weren’t just a breakthrough in speed and simplicity for laptops, they were also a bold bet on the open web as the next great computing platform. As the web becomes more walled off, and Google pivots to a platform more directly under its control, that dream has finally run its course.

How Chromebooks lost their way

The original goal for Chrome OS was to strip away all the overhead of a traditional laptop to make computing faster and easier. Here’s what Google wrote about the project in 2009:

“Speed, simplicity and security are the key aspects of Google Chrome OS. We’re designing the OS to be fast and lightweight, to start up and get you onto the web in a few seconds. The user interface is minimal to stay out of your way, and most of the user experience takes place on the web. And as we did for the Google Chrome browser, we are going back to the basics and completely redesigning the underlying security architecture of the OS so that users don’t have to deal with viruses, malware and security updates. It should just work.”

The first Chromebooks, which arrived in 2011, were basically just laptops that ran the Chrome browser, plus some extra window dressing. They had minimal internal storage and couldn’t run regular desktop software, but this allowed them to stay nimble, with speedy boot times, frictionless software updates, and minimal risk of malware. If a user lost their Chromebook, they could simply set up a new one and pick up where they left off.

In essence, Google was betting that nearly everything people did with their laptops would happen in a browser through sites like Gmail and Google Docs, so they could cut out all the other bloat to make those web apps shine.

To that end, Google encouraged app makers to build for the open web, with applications that could run in any browser, Chromebooks included. Although Google maintained a “Chrome Web Store” for web apps and extensions, the platform was only limited by the web itself. Anything you could run in a browser, you could run on a Chromebook, and that benefitted Google because it meant more people were using its search engine to find things.

“[A]ny time our users have a better computing experience [with Chrome OS], Google benefits as well by having happier users who are more likely to spend time on the Internet,” the company wrote in its 2008 blog post.

Over time, Google wavered on that original vision. It brought Android apps to Chrome OS in 2016, then added support for Linux apps in 2018. It even made a big foray into installable high-end gaming with Steam support.

While these inclusions made Chromebooks more capable, they also added new layers of complexity and demanded laptops with more storage. Setting up a new Chromebook became more of an ordeal, and preserving security became a bigger challenge. In shifting away from laptops powered by the open web, Chrome OS became exactly the kind of heavyweight computing experience it was trying to replace.

All this helped open the door for a new operating system built on Android instead. While Googlebooks will include a desktop-class version of Chrome, the emphasis now is on running Android apps and using AI.

Meanwhile, the original tenets of ChromeOS have disappeared. Look through Google’s announcement post for Googlebooks, and you will not find the words “speed,” “simplicity,” or “security” mentioned even once.

Times have changed, and so has Google

Google’s pivot away from a web-based operating system shouldn’t come as a major surprise. After all, Googlebooks are arriving at a time when the open web is destabilizing, in part because of Google itself.

Along with other tech companies that are all-in on AI, Google is betting on a world where browsing the web is increasingly unnecessary. Instead of using Google Search as a gateway to other sites, Google intends to have AI generate whatever information you need. Instead of managing your own email inbox, chatbots like Gemini will manage it for you. Instead of visiting websites to shop or make restaurant reservations, AI companies want to deploy fleets of AI agents to navigate those sites on your behalf.

As a result, using the web as a human is becoming more difficult. A growing number of websites are blocking themselves off from search engines and archival services in an attempt to keep AI crawlers out. Amazon has been limiting how many customer reviews some users can read because it thinks their behavior looks too robotic. Even just proving that you’re not a bot requires increasingly complicated steps, as in Google’s new ReCAPTCHA systems that demand phone-based verification or a recording of yourself performing hand gestures.

It’d be wrong to say that Google’s strategy with Chromebooks had anything to do with this. The company faltered on its original vision for a variety of other reasons, and the rise of AI would have been inevitable anyway.

Still, the arrival of Googlebooks serves as one final reminder of what we’ve lost. There was a time when Google believed in the open web more than anything, and it was committed to a platform with no real boundaries.

But that was back when getting folks to spend more time on the web was Google’s ultimate goal. Googlebooks exist for a world in which Google is clawing back more of that time for itself.

title: Can Apple keep its AirPods from becoming ‘PervertPods’?
description:
Apple’s AirPods are arguably the most iconic headphones ever. The small, glossy, stylish buds are lauded for both their sound and design and are worn by hundreds of millions of people across the globe. 

But come next year, those hundreds of millions of AirPods owners might face a problem they never envisioned: being labeled as creeps or perverts—all for innocuously wearing one of the most instantly recognizable tech gadgets ever made.

That’s because Apple will reportedly release a new AirPods model in 2027 with built-in cameras. Doing so poses an existential threat to the brand reputation of Apple’s most successful product since the iPhone.

From ‘glasshole’ accessory to ‘pervert glasses’

If there’s one thing that can be said about wearables with built-in cameras, it’s that the public has a deep mistrust of the people wearing them. This is because, historically, many camera-enabled wearables have done a poor job communicating to bystanders when the wearer is recording them. It doesn’t help that wearers can often disable or obscure the public-facing alerts manufacturers build into these devices that let others know they may be being recorded.

This uncertainty has caused many people, unjustly or not, to assume the person wearing the wearable is a creep or pervert, and indeed, entire terms have arisen to pejoratively describe such wearers. 

In the early 2010s, people quickly labeled Google Glass wearers “glassholes.” In the 2020s, anyone wearing Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses is often deemed to be wearing “pervert glasses.” When it came to Google Glass, the glasshole blowback got so bad that Google posted a reminder to Glass wearers not to be creepy. 

“[Don’t ]Be creepy or rude (aka, a ‘Glasshole’),” the company wrote in a tip sheet to its users in 2014. “Respect others and if they have questions about Glass don’t get snappy. Be polite and explain what Glass does and remember, a quick demo can go a long way. In places where cell phone cameras aren’t allowed, the same rules will apply to Glass. If you’re asked to turn your phone off, turn Glass off as well.”

But while a “glasshole” implies you were merely being a disrespectful jerk, the “pervert glasses” label applied to Meta’s smart glasses implies something much worse. And indeed, there is no shortage of reports that some wearers of Meta’s smart glasses are using them in privacy-invasive, nonconsensual ways.

Now, concerns about the misuse of so-called “pervert glasses” have become so widespread that there are calls in multiple countries to introduce legislation banning or limiting their use. Meta is preemptively even working on a “kill switch” feature to disable the camera capabilities of its glasses, and has already updated its software to automatically stop recording if someone covers the recording warning light on the frames.

Meta’s moves to reassure the public and governments may be too little, too late, however. The device’s reputation may already be tarnished beyond repair. Indeed, some of Meta’s own smart glasses customers already seem to think so. Owners are reportedly leaving them at home to avoid public shame and being labeled as perverts.

And that’s a problem for Apple’s AirPods—and every person who wears them.

Are all AirPods about to be labeled ‘PervertPods’?

For years now, reports have suggested Apple was working on AirPods with built-in cameras. In August, MacRumors published a video made by Apple confirming such a device is in the works. In the video, a man wearing the camera-equipped AirPods asks the devices to identify and remember the name of a book he is holding.

Bloomberg says these AirPods are on track for a 2027 release. But once they go on sale, if the public blowback against Meta’s “pervert glasses” is anything to go by, owners of even existing AirPods are potentially set to become social pariahs overnight.

This is because, unlike Meta’s smart glasses, which are obviously bulkier than the “dumb” frames people have worn for centuries, the camera-equipped AirPods shown off in Apple’s video look nearly identical to today’s AirPods: small, shiny white buds. That means any public backlash against the camera-equipped AirPods is likely to hit all AirPods users. The AirPods are already so small; who can really tell which model you are wearing?

Once camera-equipped AirPods go on sale, it’s reasonable to assume that, because they look indistinguishable from other models, bystanders will not be able to tell whether someone is wearing the camera models or the regular ones. As a result, they may become suspicious of all AirPods users.

Suddenly, someone wearing AirPods Pro 2 (from 2023) or AirPods 4 (from 2024) may get distrustful or even contemptuous looks from bystanders. In other words, the inevitable “PervertPods” label wouldn’t be limited to camera-equipped 2027 models and above. Such a label would tarnish the entire AirPods brand and make people cautious of users no matter which model they use.

Can Apple prevent AirPods backlash?

So, how can Apple stop this brand destruction?

It doesn’t have many good options. Perhaps the most practical one would be to make the camera-equipped AirPods visually distinguishable at a glance from non-camera-equipped AirPods. Apple could do this by making the camera-equipped AirPods a different color, like midnight blue or cosmic orange. 

However, it’s unlikely that Apple would be willing to ditch the AirPods’ now-iconic shiny white color scheme.

Short of this, Apple will probably rely on changing public perception: educating the public that its camera-equipped AirPods can’t save video and are used only to recognize objects (if that’s what the devices will indeed do). 

But this may not be enough. Apple gave its new Apple Watches, introduced last month, the ability to always record surrounding conversations. The company highlighted that these recordings were never accessible to Apple or the users, and once they had been processed by Siri AI, they would be deleted. Yet despite Apple designing the feature to be privacy-preserving, even the company’s own fan base has expressed serious reservations about it. 

This leads me to believe that, for the brand’s sake, Apple should consider scrapping the camera-equipped AirPods for now. The general public, once eager to embrace every new gadget Big Tech released, is increasingly wary of wearables becoming surveillance tools or enabling nefarious individuals to secretly monitor them. 

Given that this distrust will likely not abate anytime soon, Apple’s wisest move may be to set aside its visual ambitions for the device in favor of focusing on improving what the AirPods already do best: delivering world-class sound quality into our ears.

title: A new employee was reprimanded for drinking 1 cup of coffee a day. An expert says the drink isn’t the real problem
description:
A new employee says they were reprimanded for drinking too much coffee.

The user took to Reddit to detail the situation, which unfolded at a job they’d started only a month prior. Each morning, they used the coffee machine and company-provided K-Cups and creamers. However, one day, a floor manager called them in and told them it was not typical to drink coffee every single morning. 

“I don’t imagine my boss having anything to say that would make this situation better, and I think it would just be unnecessary trouble,” the user wrote. “I do not want to be seen as someone who picks problems with people for small things.” 

To mitigate the problem, the new employee said they will bring their own K-Cups and creamers into the office moving forward. They also plan to document future interactions with the manager. “I need this job more than anything right now so I’m willing to look the other way since I’m not in the position at the moment to make any demands,” they said. 

Office culture

Many of the user’s fellow Redditors immediately sided with them.

“Even when free, I’ve never once heard of a single person being told they’re drinking too much. Especially not at one per day; that seems bizarre,” wrote one user.

Another commented, “As an intern, I was drinking five cups a day, and nobody batted an eye. It got to the point where the office manager told me where to restock the coffee pods if I saw we were running low. This is a super weird thing for them to be concerned about.” 

Experts say the user’s now-lingering tension over coffee usage could potentially lead to a deeper issue around comfort and safety at the workplace.

According to data from a national study by the Harris Poll, 60% of American workers report currently having a toxic supervisor, with more than 60% admitting they actively avoid their boss at work. 

“This type of behavior dramatically reduces psychological safety at that workplace. As a result, that new employee is more likely to quit and more likely to engage in activity to damage the company’s reputation,” Russell Clayton, an associate professor of instruction in the School of Management at the University of South Florida, told Inc. 

According to the Harris Poll, 61% of workers plan to switch jobs because of their boss as soon as the market allows. A separate survey done by the MIT Sloan Management Review analyzed 34 million employee profiles and found that toxic culture was the strongest predictor of employee attrition and was 10.4 times more important than compensation in predicting turnover.

title: What to think about before making a big ask from your direct reports
description:
As a supervisor, you have some ability to dictate what your direct reports work on. The requests you make should typically fit their job description, though most descriptions have a catchall “other duties as assigned” attached, which is likely to cover you.

That said, the jobs you give someone generally have a particular expectation of the skills required, the hours to be worked, and the stress level associated with the tasks. If you’re going to ask someone to do something that far exceeds the norm, there are a few things you should consider first.

Are you taking advantage?

The people you supervise probably want to keep you happy. You have power over their evaluations, and your recommendation can help to propel them to a promotion or other opportunities. This means that when you ask your reports to do something, they are likely to agree.

You should make sure that when you’re making a big ask, the employee is likely to benefit rather than suffer from doing the work. For example, you have work that needs to be done, but you don’t want to put the time of a higher-priced employee onto it. If you’re going to try to save money by using a less-experienced person, you should be careful that you’re not adding a lot of extra hours or stress to their work just to cut costs.

Your reports pay attention to the hours that other people are putting in. If you ask far greater effort of them than you put in yourself, that can rankle in ways that may ultimately cause dedicated people to want to work elsewhere.

What are the long-term benefits?

When you are going to make that big ask, think about what benefits that work is likely to have for your direct report. Talk to them about those benefits when you make the request.

For example, a big project may give a newer employee a chance to work with senior leaders, or do work that is visible to them. That can help bring them future opportunities. A significant project may also help them to expand their capacities by taking on new experiences. That project may also lead to overtime (depending on how they are paid), allowing them to take home more money.

One reason for thinking through the benefits of this additional work for an employee is that you may discover that the assignment might be more beneficial for another member of your team. The more you can use significant tasks to develop your team, the easier it is to ask them to go beyond the norm.

What will sweeten the deal?

Of course, there are also some pretty onerous tasks that someone has to take on—and you may decide that burden should fall on one of your team members. In this situation, consider whether there are ways to make the burden less significant.

If the job is going to require additional travel or a lot of extra hours, you might want to offer compensatory time off or some time with a flexible work arrangement to reward them for taking one for the team.

If you’re going to give a team member a significant responsibility that adds effort and stress to their work, consider ways to help use that to further their career. Give that person additional mentorship to accelerate their career path or provide them with chances to engage with senior leaders who might ultimately be able to find additional opportunities for them.

When you use big asks as a way to give flexibility or career benefit to your team members, you create trust. The members of your team will talk to each other, and you don’t want to get the reputation of someone who drives people hard without looking out for them. When you give people challenge as well as support, you provide a motivating environment that allows the team to excel, even under difficult circumstances.
